# Learning and retention

The aim is not to make every page a course. It is to help readers form a useful mental model and retain the few things that matter.

## Useful memory supports

- **Mental model:** a short explanation of how the parts fit together.
- **Worked example:** demonstrate a realistic path from input to outcome.
- **Retrieval prompt:** ask the reader to recall a key idea before revealing the answer.
- **Contrast:** show what to do versus what not to do, when the distinction matters.
- **Summary:** restate a small number of essential ideas in fresh, concise language.
- **Action checklist:** turn learning into a repeatable behavior.

## Make examples do work

A good example:
- is clearly labeled as real or illustrative;
- uses the same terms as the instructions;
- shows the decision or action, not just a decorative screenshot;
- explains why the outcome is correct.

Never invent a product behavior and present it as a real capability. If the source does not establish a detail, use a neutral placeholder or mark the example hypothetical.

## Knowledge checks

Use a short check only when it reinforces an important concept or catches a likely misunderstanding. Provide feedback that explains why the answer is right.

Avoid trivia, trick questions, or quizzes that merely make a page feel interactive.

## Three-things memory anchor

When appropriate, close with up to three memorable points. If the page has more than three equally critical rules, do not force an artificial limit—use a checklist or reference list instead.

## Retention honesty

A page cannot guarantee that someone will remember it. The skill can improve recall conditions, but actual retention requires observation or testing with real readers.
